within the gut are all powerful satiety cues. They bring a meal to an end and, for a time, inhibit further consumption. Eventually,
hunger again prevails and food intake follows. The ﬂux between hunger and satiety is episodic and underpins the expression of our
eating behavior throughout the day. However, it is not just the absence of episodic satiety cues (e.g., stomach distension and intes-
tinal or absorbed nutrients) that inﬂuences the expression of hunger. Reduction in blood glucose levels or in the levels of the circu-
lating adipose tissue hormone leptin indicates a deﬁcit in available energy and in energy reserves. Such events are linked with
feelings of hunger. Fluctuation of these factors indicates the metabolism and storage of the body’s energy reserves. These are a tonic
class of physiological signals that also inﬂuence the expression of appetite. Like episodic satiety signals, these tonic signals normally
act on inhibitory mechanisms with the hypothalamus (anorexogenic circuits). Their absence elicits an active feeding response.
Other tonic factors that indicate the body’s energy status, such as adiponectin, cytokines, and gonadal hormones, also appear to
act on energy regulator centers within the brain, particularly the hypothalamus, mainly to suppress hunger. Again, their absence
serves to unleash appetite.
However, not all physiological signals, episodic or tonic, inhibit hunger. For instance, blood levels of the gut hormone ghrelin
